Ancient History.Prehistoric India:
INTRODUCTION
Prehistory refers to the period before the invention of writing. It is reconstructed through archaeological evidence such as stone tools, bones, plant remains, habitation sites and rock paintings. It represents the earliest stage of human cultural development in the Indian subcontinent.

PALEOLITHIC AGE
The Paleolithic Age or Old Stone Age is the earliest phase of prehistory. It broadly extended from about 2.5 million years ago to around 10000 BCE. Human life during this phase was marked by complete dependence on nature and a food gathering economy.

FEATURES
• Stone tools were the main cultural remains
• Tools were made mainly of quartzite and other hard stones
• Human groups lived a nomadic life in search of food and water
• There was no agriculture and no permanent settlement
• Caves and rock shelters were used at some places for habitation
• Fire was known in the later stages and helped in cooking, warmth and protection
• The Paleolithic phase is divided into Lower, Middle and Upper Paleolithic on the basis of tool development

The Lower Paleolithic phase is associated with large tools such as hand axes, cleavers and choppers. The Middle Paleolithic phase shows greater use of flake tools. The Upper Paleolithic phase reflects blade tools, improved hunting methods and early artistic expression.

IMPORTANT SITES
• Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh is known for rock shelters and rock paintings
• Hunsgi in Karnataka is important for settlement evidence near raw material zones
• Kurnool caves in Andhra Pradesh show cave habitation
• Belan Valley in Uttar Pradesh reflects a long cultural sequence
• Didwana in Rajasthan is an important Paleolithic region

MESOLITHIC AGE
The Mesolithic Age or Middle Stone Age represents a transitional stage between the Paleolithic and Neolithic phases. It broadly dates from about 10000 BCE to 6000 BCE. This phase developed in the context of post Ice Age climatic improvement.

FEATURES
• Microliths are the most distinctive feature of this phase
• Small tools were often fixed into wood or bone to make composite tools
• Hunting and gathering continued, but fishing became more important
• Semi sedentary settlements began to appear in some areas
• Early animal domestication can be seen, especially dog
• Burials with grave goods indicate the beginning of social customs and belief systems

The Mesolithic phase was a stage of adaptation and experimentation. It did not completely break with the Paleolithic way of life, but it prepared the ground for food production.

IMPORTANT SITES
• Bagor in Rajasthan is famous for animal domestication
• Langhnaj in Gujarat shows hunting and food gathering patterns
• Sarai Nahar Rai in Uttar Pradesh is known for burial evidence
• Mahadaha in Uttar Pradesh is another important Mesolithic site
• Adamgarh in Madhya Pradesh reflects continuity of microlithic culture

NEOLITHIC AGE
The Neolithic Age or New Stone Age marks a major turning point because it introduced food production. In the Indian subcontinent, Neolithic cultures appeared in different regions at different times from about 7000 BCE onward in some areas.

FEATURES
• Agriculture and animal domestication became the basis of life
• Polished stone tools became common
• Permanent settlements and village communities developed
• Pottery, weaving and storage of grain appeared
• Social organisation became more stable due to settled life
• Grinding stones, pestles and sickles indicate cultivation and food processing

The Neolithic phase marks the shift from food gathering to food production. This transformation is often described as the Neolithic Revolution because it fundamentally changed economy, society and settlement patterns.

IMPORTANT SITES
• Mehrgarh is one of the earliest farming settlements of the subcontinent
• Burzahom in Kashmir is famous for pit dwellings
• Gufkral in Kashmir is another important Neolithic site
• Chirand in Bihar shows settled life and farming activity
• Hallur in Karnataka reflects the southern spread of Neolithic culture
• Maski is also important for South Indian Neolithic evidence

REGIONAL PATTERN
In the north west, Mehrgarh gives evidence of early farming and domesticated animals. In Kashmir, pit dwellings and distinctive burial practices are striking features. In eastern India, Chirand reflects farming and settled village life. In South India, cattle keeping, polished stone axes and ash mounds are important markers of Neolithic development.

SIGNIFICANCE
Prehistoric India shows the long transition from dependence on nature to increasing control over resources. The shift from hunting and gathering to agriculture led to food surplus, population growth and stable settlements. This laid the basis for craft production, social differentiation and the eventual rise of complex civilizations.

IMPORTANT POINTS
• Paleolithic culture is identified mainly through large stone tools and hunting gathering economy
• Mesolithic culture is identified through microliths and transitional subsistence pattern
• Neolithic culture is identified through agriculture, animal domestication, polished tools and settled life
• Bhimbetka is important for rock art and long continuity of occupation
• Mehrgarh is crucial for earliest farming evidence in the subcontinent
• Burzahom is known for pit dwellings and is often important for factual questions

PYQ TRAP
UPSC often confuses microliths, polished tools and agriculture. Microliths are mainly associated with the Mesolithic phase. Polished stone tools and settled agriculture are associated with the Neolithic phase.

CONCLUSION
Prehistoric India laid the broad foundation for later cultural and civilizational development. The gradual movement from food gathering to food production remains one of the most important transitions in human history.
